en: In that machine of the body, which is made firm by the Self consisting of all the paths, [the individual] is impelled by the conscious Self— [as described in] the *Svātantryadīpikāsūtra* with its commentary composed by Manasārāma.
It moves about like the air in a bellows;
but upon the exhaustion of those karmas, when the bodily machine undergoes a change, the life-force machine disintegrates and the body becomes like a wall.
The supreme subject is indestructible.

The inner self (pratyagātman), which is of the nature of consciousness and bliss, is the witness of those two; it is celebrated in all the Upaniṣads, established through the methods of agreement and difference as being devoid of birth and death,
distinct from the [sheaths] beginning with the "food-made" (annamaya), and experienced by everyone.

"Having stated, 'The supreme person in this body is called the witness, the consenter, the supporter, the enjoyer, the Great Lord, and also the Supreme Self,' it is established that the supreme cognizer is imperishable."
Indeed, there is no loss whatsoever for the knower upon the destruction of the body,
just as there is none for space when a jar is destroyed;
for just as space remains situated both inside and outside jars, it is distinct from its limiting adjuncts.
Likewise, the cognizer within bodies is free from those limiting adjuncts, possesses an imperishable nature, is the vitalizing breath of all, and is the illuminator of everything; for this reason.
The sun of pure consciousness is the light of all.
The sun of consciousness (*saṃvin-mārtāṇḍa*), which animates the clusters of objects appearing as corpses,
illumines the entire multitude of existents through its own power of self-manifestation; for nothing whatsoever can manifest without entering into the light of ultimate consciousness.
That which manifests as whatever external or internal thing whatsoever is established as being of the nature of one's own self; for that very thing is the light that illuminates it.
As it was said by the Great Teachers:

How can he who always illuminates the reality submerged within the interior of the great cave by means of the lamp of the power of knowledge be praised as "Śiva," since he is thus the Self of the universe?
That power of Savitṛ which, within its own internal consciousness, illumines the entire collection of objects reflected therein, is itself reflected in all things;
though one, it appears in manifold forms, just as the sky [appears] in jars.

Alternatively, just as the light of the sun appears in various forms within both transparent and non-transparent objects, so too is the power of the Lord (bhagavat-śakti) of an exceedingly difficult-to-comprehend nature; if indeed the inner self (pratyagātman) is that very [power] which resides in the sun within the sky that adorns the expanse of the firmament of consciousness (cidgaganābhoga).
Residing within the cavity of the earth’s womb, that very consciousness is like the belly of a worm.

Having raised the objection: "If [the nature of all] is indeed uniform according to this statement, then why is there a distinction in bringing about the identity with the Supreme Lord for human beings as compared to animals and the like? he says:
Because of the instruction on the inclusion [of phonemes] at the beginning and the end.

The Great Lord, established from the very beginning, [perceives] the contraction ending with the earth, the insentience of intention extending from stones up to human beings, and the difference in nature among all things due to the gradation of expansion; indeed, this is the nature of insentience.

The human body is thus included within the ninefold nature; for this reason, it is the vessel that receives the light of the manifestation of the Primordial God. Like the moth in the flame, the human state culminates in the *bindu*, which consists precisely in the encapsulation of the letters *a* and *ha*.
Just as with the instruction on the secret [teaching], so it is with the other.
Through purity and impurity, one attains the status of a lord of men.
Arising from the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, it is like a sprouting shoot, characterized by swelling, dominated by *sattva*, the locus for the illumination of vision and action,
consisting of its own essential nature, and having attained existence through the internal and external organs; such is that which is intended [by the term].
Because its essential nature consists of emerging and submerging within the self-reflection of one's own conscious self,
it is characterized by the distinction between the pure and the impure; as for the human being, it is said that by bringing the reflection of Māyā under control,
one becomes the omniscient Lord (Īśvara).
But another, being under the sway of ignorance, becomes manifold due to its diversity.

For the Lord, the manifestation of vision and action occurs simultaneously with equal operation; for the individual soul (nara), however, it is the reverse. Even in the Pratyabhijñā, there is a loss of sovereignty for consciousness.

This impurity of the individual soul (*āṇavamala*) is twofold: it consists in the non-awareness of even one's own freedom (*svātantrya*), due to the loss of one's true nature. Thus, by the word "man" (*nara*), only those distinguished by the human species are meant, and not animals, trees, and so forth; for their state is determined by the varying proportions of *rajas* and *tamas*.

Regarding that which was described as the production of diversity: when knowledge arises as a manifestation through all the gates in this body, then that is called *vidyā* (knowledge); furthermore, when *sattva* has increased, there is greed.
Activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing—
these arise when rajas has increased, O descendant of Kuru. Lack of illumination, activity, negligence, and even delusion [arise when tamas has increased].
"When tamas has increased, O bull of the Bharatas, these [qualities] arise.
For this very one is the Lord, endowed with attributes such as omniscience and possessed of all sovereignty;
He alone is the inner controller (antaryāmī), the vitalizer of all, and the knower of everything.

Because its own nature is not made an object by anything else, it is the witness everywhere; in the case of the Lord, knowledge and action reside in his own essential forms, while in the bound soul (paśu), those same two—along with Māyā as the third—are established as sattva, rajas, and tamas. Thus, although the individual soul (jīva) is full [of these], it is [perceived] through these qualities which have become contracted.

Though endowed with all-knowingness and other qualities, he appears as if incomplete because of the non-recognition of his own true nature; yet, in reality, he remains that very same essence. As they say:
Through entry, one becomes identical with that.
When, at the moment of terror, one enters the abode of the Fourth (turya) by virtue of emerging into one's own essential nature,
all [limited] powers are withdrawn as if entering the heart; thus, through the play of the perfection of vision and action, the poverty of contraction is cast off.
Having cast aside [all else], the sovereignty of one's own consciousness is attained. Just as a worm,

by means of entering into meditation upon them in the form of withdrawing from everything, causes the six qualities of a bee— which were contracted within itself— to expand and becomes that very form, so too does the individual soul (jīva).

When, through the power of contemplation, Śiva— whose own manifestation of power has blossomed and who has attained the state of identity with the Supreme Lord— laughs by means of the essential nature of bestowing his own self-identity; at that time...
Upon entering the central channel, he remains absorbed in that very state; even while residing in the body,
he abides as nothing other than the nature of the sky of consciousness— free from limitations and devoid of differentiation— that true reality which is his own innate nature.
How and where can that which is distinguished by the distinction between pure and impure be characterized?
In the moon, the sun, and the fire.
Just as the Lord, the stainless and immutable deity whose nature is unobscured,
[manifests] from his own essence of the equilibrium of light and bliss an incarnation known as the venerable Anāhata, which consists of twelve digits (kalās).
In the space of one's own Self, which serves as the foundational wall, [the Lord] manifests that which is composed of His own powers; thus,

in the midst of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the individual and universal states, and of the manifestation of the persistence of both the unobscured and the obscured Self, He appears as the fire of *umā*.
By those two, [the breath] becomes pervasive, consisting of the five powers,
the locus of the fivefold inherence, the illuminator of the functions, and endowed with twelve digits,
once primordial consciousness has transformed into vital breath.

According to this principle, [the text] states that Parāśakti, having established her station in the abode of these three, causes the descent of the thousand-rayed [sun], whose nature consists of the operations of both the universal and the particular, to arise within the space of Mūlaprakṛti. Thus it says:
That is the power of the self.

But this Supreme Power (Parāśakti), having embraced the multitude of sounds (śabdarāśi) and having drawn that Kuṇḍalinī— which consists of the three coils of Parā, Parāparā, and Aparā, along with the half-coil— into her own self,
[manifests] the entire phenomenal world through the activities of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other deities.
Due to its crookedness, the fluctuation of the mind flows in a tortuous manner; through its subjection to that [mind],
all living beings— having forgotten their own conscious self— become partakers in the experience of the fruits consisting of auspicious and inauspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Having become weary, he states the method for avoiding that weariness.
In the friction [of the two poles], when one contemplates the cognizer as one's own consciousness, there is supreme accomplishment.
"One should meditate there upon the union of the moon, sun, and fire with undistracted mind.
O Dear One, by means of that yoga, the central channel becomes straight;
according to this principle, for the sake of its straightening during the union of the moon, sun, and fire—

Becoming filled with the excess of one's own love, and having contemplated one's own Self as the substrate of all through the method of *nayukti*, one brings that [Self] to a state of straightness by subduing its curved form, through entry into the Supreme Sound (*paranāda*).
One meditates upon the upward movement; through that upward movement, one causes to arise the surging bliss consisting of the supreme union, as it has been said:
"Having entered the middle path, which moves unnoticed by both Light and Bliss, this [bliss] arises."
Swallowing the duality known as sun and moon,

having entered the upward resonance (nāda) and reduced the *kula* to ashes by the fire of dissolution, he who— through non-attachment (*apramāda*)— blazes within and enters the unmanifest Śiva beyond the *akula*, is indeed [the true practitioner].
Having brought about the union of the moon, sun, and fire as she desires, she remains like Īśvara, consisting of great heroic power (mahāvīryātmikā).
Through these very powers, she performs the creation, maintenance, and withdrawal of the gross, subtle, and so forth, within the range of ordinary perception.
Just as [the moon] is capable of [manifesting] the bright and dark fortnights of Soma, so too is he; for he who,
through indifference toward that conjunction, having realized true knowledge as his own self,
performs creation and the rest like a creation born of mere volition— he too is supreme.

When consciousness enters that state through the continuous contemplation of the light of awareness, all activities become means for entering the supreme abode; otherwise, they are merely like dreams until the end.
Thus, the three states of existence, the three powers, and the three cavities [are one].
Having touched upon the stimulation of the light of the fourth state (*turya*) through the ten-fold division of the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *samāna* breaths,
he now states another means for entering the supreme reality (*paratattva*) thus established.
By means of contraction and expansion.
By the power of observing one's own self-awareness,

one who brings about the simultaneous expansion and cessation of the functions of the internal and external organs necessarily attains sovereignty over the wheel of his own powers through the stimulation of the capacity of his own Self— such is the wise man.

"Beholding the inner Self with eyes turned away, one attains immortality"— by this Vedic text, it is meant that the functions of the internal and external organs are withdrawn simultaneously from all sides, like the contraction of the limbs of a tortoise. As it is said in the *Gītā*:
"And when he withdraws these [senses] from their respective objects on all sides, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, his wisdom is firmly established"— thus,
even at the time of outward expansion, by the power of their own inherent capacity, they are directed toward their respective objects.
As it has been said:
"All powers, through the channel of consciousness and worship, [arise] from the Lord of Yoga by means of their respective objects of knowledge."
Having cast [all things] into the center, he stands as a pillar of gold, the one who shines forth in the form of the universe.
He states another method:
The intentional terminology of the great purpose.
The continuous connection with the nature of ultimate consciousness— which is all-pervasive and supreme among all objects—
is the self-awareness consisting of reflective discernment regarding all investigations into words and their referents.

One should practice with constant vigilance; through the excellence of such cultivation, having dissolved the stain of doubt regarding the cessation of even the flicker of a moment, he shall enter the Supreme Abode. For one who has not attained that state due to sluggish application, all obstacles arise.
Therefore, having become steady-minded through unimpeded effort, one should abide in the repose of the supreme state. And another [instruction]:
Yoga is the effort for the arising of existence.
When existence and non-existence appear as mortal [phenomena], the emergence of being—

whose nature consists in the establishment of form— is the exertion of power (*śaktyudyama*), which is of an infallible nature (*acyutasvabhāva*) and serves as the means for immersion into the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*). That [exertion] which exists through a firm state of identity with that oneness...

One establishes one’s own nature in one’s own self, which is of an immutable essence; in every moment, amidst the particular states of dissolution and emergence, one does not deviate from that essential nature. For through well-being, effort is brought to excellence, and activities conducive to well-being are discerned through right reasoning.
Established in one's own nature.
Mental afflictions are subtle diseases born of attachment and recollection;
he alone who is skilled in the treatment of these is truly healthy. For, as it is said, "For a man dwelling on sense-objects," through the destruction of the intellect, one perishes.
Defects such as desire and anger arise precisely from attachment;
therefore, one should pacify all of them through the cultivation of non-attachment. If they arise from procreation, their opposites [should be applied].

Dispassion and the other [virtues] must be sought as its remedy through the vision of the secret; for there is but one great disease, which is delusion, and through its helplessness comes the possession by the five great elements.
Therefore, all things designated as "elements" move under the sway of delusion and madness.

For the sake of pacifying that [distraction], he remains effortlessly in his own state of light and bliss; thus he is "established in himself" (*svastha*). For the qualities such as dispassion follow one who is always attentive, like servants.
Indeed, when the mind—which consists of the five powers—is powerful and intent upon its fluctuations, anger and other such states arise.
By what power of reasoning do they necessarily proceed and pacify the heat? To this very point, he says:
Vitarka is the supreme medicine.

For solitude (*viveka*), being the cause of the nourishment of contentment, is the supreme medicine that destroys all exertion; by its grace, yogis— having abandoned the weakness consisting of the contraction of their own selves— attain supreme heroism and shine forth like sovereign emperors.

And likewise, having performed the discrimination between the real and the unreal through the reasoning of "not this, not this," and having first stilled all the factors antagonistic to dharma, one should then, by the grace of one's own consciousness, bring all the sense organs to a state of clarity and free them from agitation.
The coexistence of the qualities (guṇas) is twofold;
and regarding the sixfold neutrality in the operation, engagement, and cessation of the qualities, it was stated by the Blessed One beginning with:
"O Pāṇḍava, [know that] illumination, activity, and even delusion... and so forth.

The second [stage], ending with the words "he is said to have transcended the qualities," is the production of the outflow consisting in the accomplishment of one's desires through one's own power. In this stage, the nature of the inclination toward the qualities undergoes transformation, and that inclination, being pure, manifests in three ways at the very beginning of its activity.
That [vision], designated as *sāttvikī*, *rājasī*, and *tāmasī*,
is also ninefold through the divisions of *unmīlana* (opening), *nimīlana* (closing), and *ardhanimīlana* (half-closing),
according to which one is predominant in each case.
Furthermore, because they are connected with the functions of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, these qualities (*guṇas*) indeed possess infinite modes;

having attained their existence through their assistance, by relying on the power within them, I— having become fully absorbed in the Self which is the self-cognition of all subjects as the "I"— act according to my will.
He will indeed manifest, by His own will, the appearance of both the object of knowledge and the knower;

moreover, the very contemplation that "I am Śiva— the undivided Self whose form is filled with the universe, whose nature is perfect, independent bliss, and beautiful form"— that alone is the supreme medicine.
Having dispelled the afflictions of birth, death, and so forth for the individual soul (jīva), whose sovereignty is contracted and who is overwhelmed by the three impurities (malas),
[he effects] the abiding of one's own self within the Self alone in the immortal abode known as Paramaśiva.
He makes manifest.
For the yogi whose power has arisen is a witness here and hereafter, owing to his state of exultation and so forth.

That which effortlessly closes within itself those mental states that, acting as a foundation for worldly existence, manifest it away from its own true nature— that alone is the power of the Self; through the excellence of that power,
its intoxicated nature and so forth are witnessed by the "Ha" (the letter *ha*), just as in the case of the *sutra* (thread).

Since dreaming and waking are both employed as functions within their own respective domains, one must necessarily admit the state of being a witness (sākṣitva) in the cognizer; anticipating the objection as to how this is so, he says:
The heart is light.

Since the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) is the locus of the expansion and repose of all manifest and unmanifest mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), therefore, even that which is capable [of being known] is, by virtue of being illumined by that light,
internally attached to self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*).

He is the witness of their activity, illuminating the various classes of objects reflected here and there. As it has been said: "Just as all types of trees on the banks are reflected in a lake, so too all the multitudes of objects are reflected in the vast mirror of one's own expansive consciousness."
In such a state, because of the withdrawal of both external and internal mental fluctuations.
Disrespect toward the teacher is pride.

In negligence, in the form of the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), in the proliferation of limited accomplishments, and in that nature devoid of autonomy— therein lies the subjugation [of the self] through the force of the surging of one's own innate nobility; such is the reflection that it must be abandoned.

When, however, one perceives even the unfolding of accomplishments (*siddhi-prapañca*) as a magical illusion, like a magician [beholding his own trick], then one has ascended to the supreme reality beyond creation and dissolution. Indeed, how could one fail to effect the submergence of such a manifold of accomplishments?
"One would be able," he said.
[He is] satisfied.

When, through the drops of His sovereignty, Brahmā and the others become partakers of power, one’s own desire is fulfilled by the attainment of that Self— the radiance of one's own nature as identical with Him— and thus becomes capable of uprooting all longings.
He clarifies that very point.
Stained by the higher and the lower, it is the supreme limit.

When one has ascended to that supreme pinnacle— which is the nature of surging beyond the knowledge based on the primary elements (prakṛti) through the contemplation of single-minded focus upon the coloring of objects that serve as the locus of distraction, and through the thorough reflection on the movements of even a hair-tip of one's own body— [then liberation is attained].

The Paramahaṃsa is one who is completely free from the latent impressions (vāsanās) concerning objects of this world and the next, whether gross or subtle, expressed through internal or external speech; the text now describes his state of being.
The Paramahaṃsa is seated in the lotus posture.

Because they share a single substratum and possess the characteristics of simultaneous contraction and expansion, the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) itself is the lotus; within that very [lotus], the Supreme Swan (*paramahaṃsa*), acting as the sovereign who effects creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace, abides by means of his own power and [thereby] transcends that which has emerged.
The Great Sound (mahārāva) is sung; the gods, beginning with Brahmā, depend upon it for their existence and their very life. Thus, the wheel of power (śakticakra) alone is his body.
He now describes the true nature of such a person who dwells in the stage of the Paramahaṃsa.
The state of being without appearance.

Whatever shines externally or internally, illumined by the moon, the sun, and fire—all that is within the range of the intellect. Therein the sun does not shine, nor the moon or the stars; these lightnings do not shine there, much less this fire.
"Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines That;
that is My supreme abode, reaching which they do not return. On the basis of such scriptural statements, that [Self] is...

Because it is the unified synthesis of all powers, both sequential and collective, it is free from appearances, self-luminous, radiant, and the place of rest; it is the innate nature of that which has become the independent Self for one who has ascended to that state.
He describes the conduct that reaches the ends of the world on occasions such as the arrival of a fire.
Svācchandyam (independence):
The state of one who abides in a nature manifested by his own autonomy is the stainless "I-consciousness," which,
through the realization that "I alone am the Supreme Swan, Śiva, the ultimate cause," constitutes the reflective awareness of the "I."

Because his essential nature is everywhere unobstructed, he therefore engages in worldly activity as he desires, preceded by straightforwardness that is free from the conceptualizations of loss and gain, honor and dishonor; as it is said: "In some respects, he is the most excellent."

"In some places seen, in others like a ghost or a piśāca, the yogi wanders upon the surface of the earth wearing various guises. Thus, he describes the state of abiding in one's own nature for one who exists in such a condition.
Reeling.

The unsurpassed essence of bliss, having flooded the internal and external wheels of the senses with its fullness, is perceived as the witness of all activities— as if reeling from the intoxication of wine— by means of the function of inward-closing the eyes. As it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
Abiding in inwardness while appearing to be engaged in external activity,

he is constantly perceived as if drowsy due to exhaustion; indeed, when the forms of both internal and external fluctuations have subsided in the supreme state, does not the wonder of innate bliss overflow?

Anticipating the objection— "Since one inevitably experiences the enjoyment of *prārabdha* (karma already set in motion) during its unfolding, how can such a nature be designated as [liberation]?"— he says:
And [the moon] is both new and full.

And this power of form, which has the appearance of death, remains in the form of wonder after having satisfied the gods, ancestors, and guests, from its outward manifestation up to its final repose in the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*).
That very [power] is undeniable from the state of the supreme subject down to the limit of outward manifestation.

The Lord of Yogis, having directly realized his own excellent nature— that his own nature is eternally arisen and nourishes and sustains all beings, and that he possesses this power like the fierce sun— shines forth, thinking, "All this manifestation is mine."
There is nothing for him apart from the manifestation of his own true nature. The greatness of such a yogin is described as follows:
Bhairava is the lord of yogins.

O All-Living One, there is no form whatsoever that is not called action; the power of the Lord, transformed by time, impels the various modifications— which are the manifestations of primordial nature—
interwoven within itself, for time indeed possesses both internal and external forms.
Causing the wheel of the seven *ṛkṣas* (constellations) to revolve by moving in two directions— southward and northward—
it manifests the division of the decrease and increase of day and night through that revolution; by means of *tatis*, *muhūrtas*, and so forth, it measures the entire phenomenal expansion.
Dependent upon Him are all living beings, from the gods down to the immovable; the glorious Lord Mahābhairava is their devourer,
autonomous, and filled with the wonder and marvel of the manifestation arising from the play of the wealth of both the non-manifest and the manifest.
The Lord of Yoga, whose nature is untainted by the emergence or dissolution [of states], is everywhere filled with the wonder of his own self-luminosity; for, due to his identity with his own Self,
the Great Lord manifests his own power within the hearts of those devoted ones who have become one with him.
One who directly realizes one's own true nature is Śiva.

[Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Means for Attaining Absorption into the Expansion of the Sovereignty of the Supreme Lord," in the *Svātantryabodhadīpikā* composed by the eminent teacher, the great Mahāmaheśvara.]
Oṃ! The Supreme Power (Parāśakti) is the very nature of Maheśvara, consisting of the essence of light and bliss. She alone manifests as the Self of all; though one, she appears in manifold forms.
Indeed, all living beings are her portions, for "in this world of living beings, he who is the individual soul is a portion of Myself."
The eternal [Lord] draws forth the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in *prakṛti*;

by this state, His partial aspect—the individual soul (*jīva*)—becomes established in that form. Due to its dual nature, it attains the state of a bound animal (*paśu*), whose essential character is dependent upon the internal and external organs, which consist of the contraction of its own innate power.
The state of being turned outward is itself the condition of being a bound animal (*paśutva*) and a state of doubt; therefore,

wishing to establish the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)— which consists in the expansion of one's own power— for one who is impoverished of power because he is turned away from the Supreme Lord who is his very self, [the author] first of all...
That very Supreme Power (Parā Śakti), who has expanded her own nature as the self of the infinite universe and who constitutes the heart of the Supreme Lord, is described by being manifested.
The power of lordship is Parākalī.

The Lord Maheśvara is the locus for the expansion and repose of all powers; the Supreme Sovereign Lady (Parā Svātantrya Bhaṭṭārikā), who is eternally united with Him, is the essential fivefold power whose nature is the vital breath (prāṇa). She is the unsurpassed one, the "I" born of the Kula.

Having attained the vibration of creative surging (*spandana-ullāsa*), the Will flashes forth in the form of Knowledge and Action with the desire to manifest this [world] externally; yet, by virtue of its requirement for that external manifestation, it remains established in its own essential nature through those [powers], possessing the nature of restraining that triad and consisting of the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*).
Having manifested Prakṛti— designated as Māyā— which consists of the equilibrium of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas characterized by contraction— and which is essentially Śiva and Śakti,
he assumes the state of being the seed and the womb; thus, by the statement "he himself is the son," he becomes his own partial manifestation.

The two lineages known as Nara and Īśvara, having projected singular and manifold forms through the opening and closing of autonomy, shine appropriately with their blossoming rays upon those various specific locations whose nature is the swelling of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), like the sun and moon amidst the darkness.

Consisting of fire, she—through those [energies] whose nature is expansion, maintenance, and withdrawal—projects, establishes, and devours this entire world of "this-ness" (idantā); thus she is Kālī. She is twelve-fold, the producer of all vidyās within all beings, and possessed of all arts (kalāvatī) due to her skillfulness.

There, in the seat of the *dvādaśānta*, she is the nature of the pervaded and the pervader; in the place of the heart, she is the treasury of knowledge (*jñānanidhi*) whose activity is life itself. Thus, at the *dvādaśānta*, she is the impulse known as Will (*icchā*), like a garland of consciousness-threads within the internal and external organs.

Having transferred knowledge and action, it manifests that magical illusion consisting of their activity; and like a blacksmith, by impelling the mechanism of the vital breaths at the seat of the heart, it kindles Vaiśvānara located within the belly.

Through the differentiation of essence and non-essence, it digests food and drink; then that which is devoid of essence is led to the location of the liver (*yakṛt*). There too, having again differentiated between essence and non-essence, that essence—by way of its own nature as the radiance of *marīci* and as the specific form of those respective powers—is [distributed] to its various locations accordingly.
It draws forth the fit [object], and by making the digit of the moon (somakalā) powerful,

it nourishes all the subtle constituents (sarvāṇuṅga); therein lie the powers of withdrawal (hāna), concentration (samādhāna), immobilization (stambhana), and the attainment of equilibrium (sāmyāpādana).

Shining with the five powers whose nature is that of the pervasive substratum, vitality itself consists of the power characterized by the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the moon and fire.
Having established the foundation in the midst of the Moon, Sun, and Fire,

consisting of the nature of the thirty-six *kalās*— in this manner, Consciousness alone has pervaded everywhere from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) down to the mouth; one who is turned away from that is a bound soul (*paśu*).
He says that very thing:
Due to its aversion [to reality], the living being is subject to the power of others.

According to the principle that "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings," the Supreme Consciousness alone is the Self within the hearts of all; yet, due to its primary nature— which consists in the forgetting of its own essential being— its innate power and majesty become contracted, and this is *prakṛti*.

Having attained identity with it, the nature of consciousness transforms into vital breath (*prāṇa*); the vital breath and the mind are bound to one another, and all particularities are essentially its own modifications. These [modifications] are mostly expanded in locations such as the heart and the abdomen, each according to its respective [function].

For the living being (jīva), who assumes an identity equal to [the Supreme] by nature, abides there in accordance with the qualities (guṇas), like the relationship between milk and clarified butter; thus he is dependent on that [Supreme]. Consequently, due to the delusion caused by the wheel of phonemes (mātṛkā-cakra) whose essence is the vibration of sound, his cognition is colored by the manifestation of external objects.
Overwhelmed by the false conviction that the form [of the body] is the self,
and being overcome by desire, anger, greed, pride, envy, grief, joy,
and so forth, one is defeated by birth, death, and disease, as it has been said:
Established in sattva, established in rajas, and established in tamas— the knower of the qualities (guṇavedaka), the embodied soul (dehī) thus wanders,

going from one state to another. Suspended by the nooses of Brahmā, situated within the consciousness of the cranial aperture (karandhra), the most terrible Mistress of the Seats (pīṭheśvarī) deludes [the soul].

"Again and again," [it is said], "he is obstructed by the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), and that which was spoken of arises as a cognition. For one who has reached such a state, he now declares the means for the cessation of delusion, the attainment of one's true nature, and the removal of afflictions.
The observation of the instability of the body.

One should observe the instability of this body, which is fashioned from semen and blood, subject to the six transformations, and defiled by the ten faults. It must be contemplated as being like the current of a river or a bubble on the water. This wretched body is merely a vessel for the experience of pleasure and pain.

Perceiving that [the world] is indeed momentary and transitory, one observes that its related things— such as family and so forth— are likewise passing away; for one who has thus attained the firmness of the cultivation of the most intense dispassion, there arises the realization of the true nature which is of the essence of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*satyajñānānandasvarūpa*).
He states the reason for abiding in one's own self:
Association with the supreme.

In order to understand that [Reality], one should approach a teacher with fuel in hand— one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*); thus, according to the Śruti, having gone into the presence of those whose passion and aversion have dissolved and whose supreme awakening has blossomed, one should precede [the inquiry] with service, prostration, and so forth.
Having heard with heart and ear those words spoken by him with sincere devotion, one must act in accordance with them; for the preservation of his command is the supreme merit,
while disregarding it is a great sin, especially for those who have ascended to the ultimate reality.
Indeed, association with the virtuous is conducive to attaining the supreme state,
but not that of hypocrites who lack true knowledge; for one's own nature functions in accordance with the company one keeps, therefore it is rightly said that association with the best is essential.

Thus, those who rest in the unsurpassed state, whose hearts have been purified, and who are most excellent, are capable of delivering others from the vast ocean of existence— whether by sight or by touch— through the reasoning of the instructions of the true tradition. They shall deliver them.
It has been stated that the lords of yogins are established in the *kulācāra*;
he now clarifies the reasoning attained therein, which nourishes their abiding in their true nature.
Reasoning consists of middle-level reflection.

The yoga that consists of the contemplation of the center amidst the functions of the vital breath— such as contraction, expansion, and suspension, as well as its internal and external movements— is, by its very nature, the surging forth of consciousness;
it is the supreme consciousness (*parā-saṃvit*) whose essence is the support of all things.

This is the cause for the thorough knowledge of one's own self (*svātmaparijñāna*). Just as fire arises from the friction of wood and clarified butter (*sarpi*) emerges from the churning of milk—appearing as something distinct—so too, through the practice of contemplating the Middle Way (*madhyacintana-yukti*), the direct realization of one's own self occurs; such is the sense. Now, [one might ask]: what is the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*)?
Since there are many obstacles that hinder stability, he explains how one might pacify them:
Through the excellence of practice, obstacles are eliminated.

Through the cultivation and refinement of middle-level meditation, by restraining the fluctuations of the mind here and there, and through the non-forgetting of the contemplation of the "middle" at every moment, [one attains stability] regarding all disturbances—
whether gross or subtle— such as the afflictions of pride and the like.
Tranquility is freedom from expectation, for one whose agitation has been stilled.
From one-pointedness of mind comes the realization of the Self.

In the heart of one who has transcended lethargy, distraction, indolence, and the like; who has cast aside the proliferation of various petty supernatural powers (*siddhi*); whose nature is the stability of the *bindu* through the continuous, non-conceptualization of one-pointedness of mind;
who is endowed with contentment and other virtues; and who possesses faith and devotion.

Self-awakening, which consists of the expansion of one's own true nature, becomes the attainment of being (*sattvāpatti*) and this is the pervasion of the Self (*ātmavyāpti*). When it is said that "this alone is the fourth stage characterized by the pervasion of the Self," according to the principle that "the pervasion of Śiva is otherwise than this," when [one reaches] Śiva—
If one desires pervasion at that time, [then...]
Filled with aesthetic relish.

Just as a fish is completely filled with the essence of water, so too is his body filled by the relish of that [divine] taste— the nature of which is the reflective awareness of oneness with Him— by one who, through the firmness of the excellence of faith and devotion, desires to attain the Śaiva dharma.

Just as the activity of fish occurs effortlessly because they consist of water, so too does the activity of the intellect, mind, vital breath, and senses of yogis consist of the emergence of the perceptions of others.
For one thus engaged in yoga, that very form consists of vows and austerities.
Through the excellence of the emergence of the reflection of the Other,
one becomes the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) himself— endowed with all sovereignty and pervading both internally and externally.
That vow which consists in becoming the locus of such great pride (*mahābhimāna*) by way of this certainty— that "I alone am he"— is indeed the complete [vow].
Austerity is the essential nature of cutting away impurity; for one who partakes in such vows and austerities,
a state of grace characterized by the unfolding of sovereign power manifests everywhere,
and for this [state], there is the recitation (*japa*) which is the means for non-differentiation.

When the outward flow of internal and external discursive speech is withdrawn, one becomes the nature of the non-conceptual, with an unimpeded essence; then, when the division of the triad [of subject, object, and means] occurs, I am Śiva— the supreme vibration, whose nature is manifestation, and who is primarily the speech of Paśyantī— and thus the recitation (*japa*) arises.
When the recitation, which consists of pacification, shines forth within the heart, then—
The supreme gain is from the offering of distinctions.

The attainment— that is, the direct realization— of the Supreme Lord, who is a mass of supreme light and bliss, occurs through the casting of one's own nature into Him, following the pacification of the distinctions and non-distinctions between the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), *māyā*, the state of being a subject (*pramātṛtva*), and the internal and external mental constructs (*vikalpa*).

As it has been said: "When this quartet—the mind, the power of volition, the vital breath, and the self—is completely dissolved into the Beloved, that is the body of Bhairava," and so forth; this indeed is the form of total surrender.

By means of this *pūrṇāhuti*, the fire that consumes the impressions (*vāsanā*) of merit and demerit accumulated over many lifetimes awakens within the cavity of the *suṣumṇā*; through its mouth, the Lord of Consciousness is fully satisfied, and being thus satisfied, He [bestows] upon those possessed of devotion the form of the Great Void (*mahāvyoma*).
It bestows the supreme accomplishment; thus it is said.
Because that does not arise, there is supreme clarity.

Since the capacity to bring about equilibrium is everywhere the defining characteristic of udāna according to its respective suitability, therefore, from the nature of the arisen intermediate power (*madhyabala*), there occurs the descent of the power of the Supreme Lord— who is the abode of consciousness— consisting in the emergence of His activity and the absorption into His very self-nature.

For the udāna is indeed the great fire; just as various substances placed within a fire are reduced to the state of fire, so too, through the arising of the function of udāna, the vital breaths, the internal organs, and the rest,
by surrendering their identity to it, become truly one with Truth and Knowledge.

It has been stated that through the immersion of the state of *prāṇa* into *udāna*, there arises the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). That power, which becomes dependent upon the waking and other states due to its following after the senses such as the sense of smell, is designated as the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva-saṃvit*).

That very [consciousness], by virtue of attaining its own power within the central channel (madhyadhāmātman), becomes the fourth state (turyā)— the nature of ultimate consciousness (paramārthasaṃvitsvarūpā) beyond both upward-moving (udāna) and downward-moving (apāna) breaths—
having dissolved this entire universe, which consists of both difference and non-difference, into its own self.
That which was described as resting in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is placed within the body of the universe;

that too is placed in the heart, and that in the Person (puruṣa); that man is situated in the Bindu, and that in the profound space called Viyat; and all this is placed in that which is called Knowledge (jñāna), and that even in the glory of Supreme Bliss (paramānanda).
Following that, he describes the characteristics of rest, stating: "The conduct of existence, having the form of the great void, triumphs."
Horripilation and so forth are the signs of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Dizziness, trembling, whirling, leaping, and bliss—these are the internal signs [of samādhi] which arise sequentially;
however, due to the intensity of bliss, tears and horripilation are its external signs. That is samādhi.
In the manifestations [of consciousness], that which consists of the totality of white (pure) activity, whose nature is light and bliss, is called *samādhi*. Thus he describes its essential nature.
Through immersion, one becomes equal to the Lord.

In his well-integrated self, through the method of the *bhāla* [the forehead], he has now arisen in the state of *udānīya*; by the firmness of that, he has attained the state of identity with the Fourth (*turya*). Through that identity, in the states of waking and so forth, his own sovereignty has blossomed, and the functions of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other faculties have dissolved.

He becomes fully absorbed in the abode of Paramaśiva. Through that absorption, he shines forth like a sovereign emperor in all his states; even while living, he attains union with Śiva. As it has been said: "Oh, what a play of one's own in this saṃsāra! Oh, how easily attained is liberation!"
Good fortune! The bud of the end has been severed; oh, such is the conduct of the Śiva-yogins in their union—may there be auspiciousness!
[Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Descent of the Supreme Power," in the *Svātantryadīpikā* composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara.]
Oṃ! Just as Maheśvara, whose essential nature is the state of equilibrium between the supreme and the non-dual, by the power of his own Śakti,
having effortlessly manifested within the space of his own Self— which serves as the foundational wall for all that consists of the "this-ness"—
and then withdrawn it, abides in his own innate nature, which consists of light and bliss.
Independent, having attained identity with that suchness, and having become its very form, they are liberated while living;

being free from saṃsāra until the end of liberation, they perceive that very essence which consists of manifestation, [perceiving] Śiva and Śakti as having the nature of a gradation and their essential state as one of aesthetic harmony (sāmarasya).
First, he makes manifest the power of discernment (vimarśa-śakti) blossoming within the heart.
Shining forth, it is the Great Light.

The Lord of Consciousness, whose nature is supreme bliss and whose essence is great luminosity, shines by means of His own power of manifestation; for manifestation is indeed existence, which consists of the nature of vibration. By that manifestation, [all things] characterized as light and darkness [are revealed].

External and internal objects such as blue, pleasure, and so forth appear; however, although the light of the sun and other sources shines, it is not capable of establishing its own nature. For this reason, like the manifestation of blue and so forth, they are essentially insentient, [being manifested] by the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*).

And that [consciousness], having attained its existence, is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Now, one might ask: "On what basis is the self-luminosity of the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*) to be accepted? To this, he says:
Because it possesses the quality of discernment.

All manifestations depend upon the light of consciousness; by its illumination, both lights and darknesses shine forth. For the light of consciousness is self-luminous because it possesses reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). This so-called reflective awareness has "I" as its essential nature, as it has been said:

The manifest is not separate from the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and reflective awareness is not separate from the manifest. Reflective awareness as "I" is not other than one's own essential nature;
I am reflective awareness whose sole form is consciousness (*cit*). From this very reflective awareness alone, everything has arisen.
For reflection (*vimarśa*), which has attained its true being, is the innate, non-artificial nature of everything; and thus, in the *Pratyabhijñā*,
they know that the nature of manifestation is reflection, otherwise the object would merely be a light.

Even though crystal and other such substances are insentient by nature, they exist as reflections; thus, reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is the primary form of the Supreme Lord. Through that [reflection], the Lord, who is one's own self, must be fully known as being identical with oneself. As it has been said regarding Him, the God of gods: [the text continues].
Vimarśa, whose nature is supreme awakening, is the supreme power (paramāśakti) endowed with the knowledge of the omniscient; thus she is celebrated as Śakti.
Her form is infinite radiance.
I am the supreme power of reflective awareness (*vimarśinī-śakti*), whose nature is consciousness; manifesting in the forms of *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*,
I shine forth as the essence of will, knowledge, and action, each of which possesses three aspects.
Having manifested a ninefold creation of colors consisting of the self-luminous rays of one's own form, as well as the nature of the words and mantras identical with that,
by means of the pratyāhāra (synthetic contraction) of the letters *ka* and *ha*.

Because its essential nature is the inseparability of *nāda* and *bindu*, this very [consciousness], which has become the potency of the tenth [state], shines forth pre-eminently as the state of mind (*cittatva*). Thus it is said: "In this world, there is no cognition that exists apart from the following of sound; knowledge is, as it were, permeated by it."

Everything is understood through sound. If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, illumination would not shine forth, for that [speech] is what performs reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśinī*).
Furthermore:
And the twelve-fold Ahaṃsī.

The Blessed Consciousness itself, being of the nature of mutual vibration, is designated as Unmanā; having reached the state of Samanā, which consists of a slight volition according to the Śruti, "May she desire to create progeny," it [becomes] the gross aspect, beginning with Vyāpinī and ending with the letter 'A'.
It descends subtly in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as it has been said:
"The eleven *kalās* always move within the *prāṇa*:
the letter *A*, the letter *U*, the letter *M*, and the *bindu* itself."
The Half-moon, the Obstructress, Sound, and the End of Sound;
Power, the Pervasive One, and the Equal One is remembered as the eleventh;
then the Transmental, which transcends that, and what transcends that is the Untainted. Thus [the sequence] begins with the letter A and ends with the Bindu.

The five measures (mātrās) range from Nāda to Vyāpinī; these five portions of the measures consist of the mental resolve (saṅkalpa) whose nature is the desire to manifest externally, which is Asamanā. The presiding ground over them is Unmanā, whose nature is the supreme vibration that is not [limited by] the vital breath (prāṇa).

She is the primary power (*mukhyā-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord Haṃsa; manifesting as the radiance of her own rays, she resides between the two lotuses at the mouth of the *Arvādha* (?), filled with the intensity of love for her own Master, displaying the wonder of her own sovereign majesty (*vibhūti*).

For the sake of producing wonder, the Great Sound, consisting of twelve parts, is sung by means of the twelve great sentences (mahāvākya); for thus it is said: [The following verses would follow here: 1. *Om*—the seed-syllable of all mantras, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 2. *Ām*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 3. *Iṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 4. *Īṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 5. *Uṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 6. *Ūṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 7. *Ṛṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 8. *Ṝṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 9. *Lṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 10. *L̥ṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 11. *Eṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. 12. *Aiṃ*—the seed-syllable of the supreme mantra, the source of all, the supreme Brahman, the primordial sound, the unmanifest, the supreme state. Thus indeed is this [Great Sound].
Then it is established, having its own nature obstructed.
Just as the Supreme Lord, by virtue of His absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), possesses a nature that is unimpeded everywhere,

so too does one who has attained identity with Him— while engaged in the operations of the intellect and other faculties— not forget the play of the abundance of His own Self, thereby severing the fetters of identification with the body.

I am of the nature of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss; having the form of the realization "I am Brahman," I am the eternally manifest state of the Self. By entering such a true abode through this very nature, everything becomes immortal.
Because of the immersion into that reality— which consists of the vibration of the very existence of supreme consciousness and whose nature is truth—
everything within the sphere of body, speech, and mind is the unfolding of the Supreme Lord, who is eternal, all-pervasive, and of a perfect nature; it occurs through His absolute sovereignty.

Whatever activity proceeds through body, speech, and mind by one who has become upright on the path of heart, word, and deed, that very thing becomes manifest before him; and moreover, he [perceives] this as well.
One whose magnanimity has arisen.
For the yogi whose magnanimity has arisen, whose very nature is the emergent magnanimity of his own self-awareness,

there is no stain from the impure mud of the phenomenal world of illusion— known as the activity of the body, senses, and so forth— just as a lotus remains unstained; nor does he possess any latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of the manifestation of that activity, even for a fraction of time.

Having overcome destiny, attachment, and the rest, the existence consisting of pure *vidyā* is of a universal nature; therefore, his knowledge transcends the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), being self-established rather than dependent on the state of the deluded. It is the awakened *anuttara*.

Such a yogi illumines the thirty-six principles (tattvas), which, being his own essential nature, are marked by the character of his innate magnificence and are completely filled with the glory of his own power.
With delusion stilled, he is fortunate and free from conceptual thought.

Having realized that the activity of the three bodies (*śarīra-tritaya*), the three states (*avasthā-traya*), and that very world named the triple universe (*jagat* or *loka-traya*)— along with its shadow and its stain— is entirely of the nature of the expansion of one's own power, [one should abide] in that very place which is the station of its sovereign.

Abiding in one's own Self—which is the nature of the unchanging ultimate reality and endowed with all sovereignty—the fortunate one who has accomplished his purpose, the man of steady wisdom, sports without limit; for this world is his playground, as it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "When delusion is exhausted and duality dissolves..."

When the ocean of knowledge has been realized, when the truth has been fully understood, and when the Self has been attained by those of unerring intellect; when the noble ones have investigated all things and, through their wisdom, perceived the true nature of both existence and non-existence as having dissolved away—
then this worldly wandering becomes a sport within the heart, where the mind is serene and one’s own glory is manifest.
When the supreme state has been attained, one transcends all fragmented perceptions of worldly activity;

as the internal mental constructs subside before them through the union with the supreme bliss, this world is seen as a mere play of the Reality. The expansion of the chariot is the body, its construction is the arrangement of the elements, and its movement is the activity of the senses.

"Whether I am the supreme one, possessing unmeasured and infinite glory, or another, I wander in this world as a body of speech"— with such a stainless intellect, when reality is perceived, this worldly wandering is merely sport.
Thus, everything is of such a nature.

Knowing that the entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, rests within one's own Self— the support of all which has become the ground of existence— one moves about in this world as one liberated while living, fearless, through the pacification of passion, hatred, pride, humiliation, and the like.
One who knows reality in this way.
The space of consciousness is the state of rest.

The repose of light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva). And that very repose has been described as the cessation of all dependence, and so forth, within one's own self-nature, which is a mass of the bliss of the light of consciousness, resembling a great ocean without waves.

In the place of rest, by means of one's own self, when the bondage of agitation has dissolved and all stains of doubt— such as coming and going, liberation, and so forth— have fallen away, only the space of consciousness remains; for such indeed is it.
Before that, he is absorbed in that.

Since the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the sky of consciousness, is the all-pervading space, the support of all, and the foundational wall [of existence], therefore, even when one has attained identity with Him, at the moment of the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, one becomes composed of that very [consciousness]; for His awareness no longer flows out toward the senses and their objects as it did before. Rather—
The undivided space of consciousness remains like the sky when a jar is destroyed;
this indeed is liberation, and not a departure to any other place. Even the Śruti says: "His vital breaths do not depart;
they are absorbed right there," and "He who was already liberated is liberated once more."
He defines liberation itself by analyzing it according to its different stages.
Liberation in accordance with one's own intrinsic nature.

That consciousness which, by following the doors of sight and the other senses, takes on various names and designations as the individual soul (*jīva*), becomes the Fourth State (*turyā*) upon ascending to the level of the self-luminous cognizing subject; it is of the nature of one's own essential being, appearing in whatever way according to the degree of the unfolding of its sovereignty.

Liberation is such that one seizes the very nature [of Prakṛti]; for just as men mounted upon the vehicle of Prakṛti become independent and perfected ones, having ascended to the state of perfection, they maintain their physical bodies at will,
possessing all sovereign powers.
Having united the five elements with the Self, which is the nature of consciousness perfectly complete in its attainment, they—
possessing a nature free from obscuration and having the form of the space of consciousness— shine forth brilliantly.
Just as Śuka-deva and others, having ascended to the state of the Lord, being independent through great māyā,
fashion the construction of the body of the light of consciousness according to their own will.

I alone am supreme bliss with a body ever filled with it; all cognizing subjects are blissful by depending on a fraction of that bliss. According to the Vedic scripture, "From bliss indeed these beings are born," bliss is the nourisher of all and is preeminent in every respect.

Shining forth and being desired by Brahmā and the other gods, I— having become that very nature of "Matsya"— perform at will within my own self a play consisting of both the universe and that which transcends the universe, preceded by a sense of wonder; thus he says:
The hero stands in the center.
The internal movement consisting of the consciousness of the Lord, the thought "I know," the accomplishment [of action],
memory, exclusion, conceit, determination, volition, the internal discourse ending with the vital breath,
the resonance of each respective word, and the various vibrations of the sense organs and the organs of action.

Forms possess infinite powers; among them, those such as Hari, Hara, and others shine forth by themselves when they have dissolved their identification with the body, become indifferent toward *māyā-prakṛti*,
and rest in the state of bliss, casting off the body composed of the five elements right here at the final moment.

Just as milk, having been poured into milk, becomes merged in the supreme ether, so too do these four types of liberation, according to their respective degrees of excellence, possess infinite subdivisions here; for those endowed with sovereignty over the worlds and other such states, it is solely through the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (śaktipāta) that this occurs.
The commentary is auspicious.
[Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Liberation while Living," in the *Svātantryadīpikā* composed by the eminent teacher Śrī Mahāmaheśvara.]
Oṃ. Now, in the determination of the Fourth State (turyollāsa), the contemplation of the supreme Lord’s own essential nature is proclaimed.

I alone am the Leader and the Sovereign, established perfectly as the very nature of joy, whose nature is undivided and who has become the foundation for all. Although I am active through various means and manifesting wonder, I remain truly established in my own place, which consists of great power; indeed, there is no falling away from that state.
Thus, through the distinction of states, there is no alteration of the nature of the bliss of the Self which remains undecaying;

for these various qualities, entering as their respective functions, do not cause my non-conceptual essential nature to undergo the state of being tossed by waves, like the currents of many rivers entering the ocean— such is its inherent nature.

Established in that state and having ascended to the level of the Lord of Power, the Great Hero, whose radiant nature has not subsided, demonstrates through his power of self-illumination: "I illuminate all of that."
The manifestation of one's own power.

The Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), whose nature consists of the autonomous awareness "I am the very essence of my own being," having simultaneously manifested that multitude of infinite powers from her own essential nature— which serves as their foundational support— by her own will, through the properties of simultaneous expansion (*unmeṣa*) and contraction (*nimeṣa*).

Because it consists of that very vibration, within its own self—which is of the nature of self-luminosity and has the form of the Great Void—it quivers as "kaca-kaca. Its rays, existing in that place, consist of various activities and are designated by various powers; indeed, there is nothing whatsoever apart from that.
For she, being actionless, through her nature of sporting in various ways, having withdrawn attachment from those respective activities, and because she is of the nature of all vital breaths—
resting in the non-dual state for those intent on serving me— she [is the cause] of their activity of opening and closing the eyes.
I myself am the witness and independent; thus he said.
The Hero is present in both states.

When all the powers (*śakti*) have withdrawn their functions and flow forth as a single convergence at the opportune moment, that very state wherein the nature [of things] dissolves internally and externally in the opening and closing of the eyes— that is Sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
In that Sovereignty, I myself am Śiva, the Lord, who by the power of his own sovereignty is eternally the Lord within the auspicious (*sadā-śiveśvara*).
Having become so, I bring about their two states—consisting of closing and opening the eyes—as I desire; for there is nothing whatsoever apart from me.
This is the truth as it accords with my own view.
Having become my own essential nature— which consists of reflective awareness and has the character of light and bliss— there is existence (*sattā*),
which is the power of the supreme consciousness of one's own nature (*svarūpāparā-saṃvicchakti*); by means of that, whatever [arises]...

Whatever is manifested, whether external or internal, that very thing is established as having attained its own state; I alone am the Lord of Consciousness, and by the power of the manifestation of my own consciousness,
[I constitute] the subjects and the means of knowledge from Brahmā down to an ant.

Having manifested this entire universe, which consists of objects of knowledge, within the space of one's own Self that serves as its foundation, I manifest as various names and designations according to their respective natures; thus they say.
He alone is the locus of perception.
There is no difference in this Self from the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) and so forth due to the distinctions of mental apprehension;
rather, it exists through the very state of being the "I" of this creation, according to the principle that "just as fire exists within wood, so does [the Self] exist within karma.

Thus, it is the vital breath of all within the manifold variety of the universe—which consists of both means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*)—and which takes on various states as its own nature.

I am the supreme, singular perceiver, whose nature is *svacchanda*; like an actor, I sport through various states, yet there is no alteration in the nature of that living being, because my essential nature is the single reflective awareness of "I. This cognition of "I" is present everywhere.
Having an obstructed nature and being an impeller everywhere—this very point he clarifies.
Everything is subject to my command.

I alone, having expanded my own sovereign power everywhere as is appropriate, dwell as the supreme emperor in the three worlds; for indeed, without my impulsion, no one anywhere engages in their own activity. I alone, as the vital breath in all beings, having assumed the form of this or that deity in each respective place by means of my own inherent power—
I perform that various activity, consisting of both sequential and non-sequential modes, according to my will;
yet there is no agitation whatsoever in my nature, which consists of supreme bliss and pervades those various states.
For me, who am independent, there is no movement anywhere. Thus they say:
I am full; I am content.

I alone am that [reality], for in all states I am filled with the essence of the aesthetic relish (*rasa*) of the supreme awareness (*parāmarśa*)— the wonder and marvel of the expansion of my own sovereign power (*nijavibhūti*)— due to being both the pervaded and the pervader. Thus, satisfied within my own self whose nature is profound and pure, I am therefore free from [all limitations].

Because it is untainted by any agitation whatsoever, my own nature—which is eternally risen *saccidānanda* (existence-consciousness-bliss)—shines forth with supreme excellence; for even while consisting of the universe, it transcends the universe. Therefore, I say:
My nature is devoid of limiting adjuncts.

My own nature is the Great Space— pure, stainless, and free from all limiting adjuncts— which is the very essence of the conceptualization of Śiva, Ātman, Jīva, Īśvara, and Brahman, and which is devoid of the power of transformation regarding bondage and liberation, as well as enemies, friends, home, wife, and so forth.

I am of the nature of reflective awareness, the essence of supreme bliss and consciousness; because my own nature is free from all limiting adjuncts, like the fierce sun, I abide in my own state of perfect tranquility, manifesting the wondrous play that consists of the universe while simultaneously transcending it.
For this reason, I am filled with wonder.
I am Śiva, the autonomous one.

I alone am the Great Space, the mass of supreme bliss, the Lord of Consciousness; though consisting of the universe, I transcend the universe, and though transcending the universe, I manifest as the play of my own expansive power— the very nature of which consists of the universe— through the forms of both succession and non-succession.

Just as, having fashioned one's own desire within the pure supreme space that consists of the expansion of one's own radiance, one shines intensely within one's very self through the excellence of one's own sovereignty; for the sovereign self, shining forth, indeed becomes intoxicated by its own internal nature.
In the power-seat (śaktipīṭha) of the essence of consciousness, I am Bhairava, the Great Bliss, who craves the union of the couple (yāmala-vṛtti);
"I am Śiva"—thus [ends] the auspicious [text].
[Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Overflowing of the Power of Sovereignty," in the *Svātantryadīpikā* composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara.]
This *Svātantryadīpikā* was composed by the Great Māheśvara teacher Maṇḍanārāma for the benefit of people.
